title: Adaptive Memory Retention in Dynamic Graphs
one_liner: A dynamic graph model that keeps useful information flowing across nodes while actively removing noise, using math inspired by physics systems that conserve energy.
lead: Real-world networks change over time — social graphs grow, communication links appear and disappear, sensor readings arrive one frame at a time. The challenge is to learn patterns across these timesteps without letting noise pile up. This paper introduces LAMP, which adds a 'drain' mechanism that forgets less-useful information at each layer, letting the model see far into the past without drowning in accumulated junk.

paras: When you stack many graph layers, each one reads what previous layers computed and sends a message to neighbors. But here's the trap: at each layer, every node collects messages from all its neighbors, not just the useful ones. Useful messages carry real patterns; useless ones are random noise from that step. A naive model would just add all messages together, so noise from layer 1 feeds into layer 2, which adds its own noise, which feeds into layer 3... After ten layers, the noise is so loud that the real signal is buried.

Dynamic graphs make this worse. A node might receive a message from a neighbor that was relevant three timesteps ago but is stale now. A naive model would weigh it equally with fresh, recent information. So information accumulates without control — the model cannot distinguish signal from historical junk.

callout.html: Information flowing through graph layers accumulates noise over distance and time, making it hard for the model to learn stable patterns.

panels.title: 1. Messages arrive

panels.title: 2. Noise piles up across layers
panels.caption: Layer by layer, noise accumulates. The signal drowns in accumulated junk.

panels.title: 3. Dissipation drain opens
panels.caption: The learned drain mechanism forgets what is not useful for the task.

panels.title: 4. Stable flow maintained

panels.caption: Conservative flow keeps signal paths open; dissipation removes noise trails.

panels.title: 5. Long-range patterns clear
panels.caption: The model sees deep into the past without the noise that buried earlier layers.

steps.text: Each node collects messages from its neighbors at the current timestep.
A principled flow preserves the true signal: it does not let information leak sideways or pile up randomly.
A second pathway learns which information is noise for your task and actively removes it.
Both pathways (keep and forget) apply at each layer and each timestep independently.
Messages from ten layers back arrive clear and useful instead of drowned and distorted.

paras: The paper adds a second, learnable pathway that actively forgets information. The first pathway is conservative: it preserves all information, designed by math to never distort the signal. The second pathway is dissipative: it learns what information is useless noise for your particular task and gradually removes it. Both run in parallel at every layer and timestep.

hidden.name: learned dissipation rate
paras: The dissipation strength is a number the model learns during training that controls how much to forget at each layer. A high number means aggressive forgetting — only the strongest signals survive. A low number means almost everything is kept. The paper does not prescribe this number; instead, it learns from data which signals matter for your task.

The model estimates dissipation by comparing what happens when you propagate information through a layer with and without the drain. If removing a signal changes the loss (the error on your task), that signal was important and dissipation should be low. If removing it does not change the loss, dissipation can be high — that information was noise anyway.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger dissipation (forgetting). Highlighted nodes are actively learned to be forgotten at that layer.

reads.html: Think of a conversation in a busy room: some voices carry important information (your friend speaking), others are background chatter. Dissipation is the process of your brain learning to tune out the chatter and amplify the friend.

The paper sets up dissipation using antisymmetric matrices (square tables of numbers arranged so they flip sign when you flip them) and data-driven control, yielding a learned decay rate per layer that balances information retention with noise suppression.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: conservative flow plus learned forgetting
paras: The core move is to split information flow into two independent channels. The first channel is conservative: it is designed using math from physics (a special structure where numbers flip sign when you flip rows and columns) to preserve all information without distortion or leaking sideways. The second channel is dissipative: it learns which information matters for your task and removes the rest by reducing its strength at each layer.

Why does this avoid noise buildup? Because the conservative channel ensures no signal leaks or gets distorted, and the dissipative channel actively removes what is not useful. Layer by layer, useless information is reduced, so noise does not accumulate. Useful signals are preserved by the conservative channel and stay clear all the way to the output.

stages.s: Conservative flow keeps all information, undistorted
Apply at every layer and timestep
Clear signal, stable across many layers

math.h2: The equation: conservative flow plus dissipative loss
math.words: The change in node values at each timestep is the sum of a conservative part (which keeps information) and a dissipative part (which removes it). The conservative part is antisymmetric, meaning it does not let information leak sideways. The dissipative part is designed to be smooth and data-driven, learning what to forget.
math.equation: dx/dt = A(x) + D(x, theta)  where A is antisymmetric (conserves flow) and D is dissipative (removes learned-to-be-useless information)
symbols: the node values (representation) at this timestep
how the node values change over time (one step)
the conservative part: how messages flow without leaking, using antisymmetric math
the dissipative part: how much each node value is reduced, learned from your data
the learnable parameters that control which information to forget

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Node A has value 10, representing a strong recent message.
Node B has value 2, representing weak noise from three layers back.
Conservative flow A(x) passes both through: node A stays 10, node B stays 2 (nothing lost).
Dissipation D(x, theta) learns that messages like B's are noise. It reduces B by 80% per layer.
After one layer: node A is still 10, node B drops to 2 * 0.2 = 0.4.
After two layers: node A is still 10, node B drops to 0.4 * 0.2 = 0.08 (nearly gone).
After three layers: node A is still 10, node B is 0.008 (truly vanished).
Node A's signal stays clear because it was never noise to forget; node B is gone because the model learned it does not matter for the task.

math.note: The conservative channel never leaks information sideways and preserves all flow; the dissipative channel learns to shrink whatever is not useful for your task.

charts.title: Naive stacking
charts.note: Without dissipation, noise accumulates and accuracy collapses at deep layers.

charts.title: LAMP with learned dissipation
charts.note: With dissipation, accuracy stays high all the way down. Long-range patterns are clear and useful.

items.html: If the model learns to forget too much, it removes real signal along with noise. The model becomes unable to see long-range patterns because it is forgetting them.
If the model does not learn to forget enough, noise still accumulates and swamps the signal. Stability is not improved.
Dissipation is learned for one task. If you apply the trained model to a different task where 'noise' suddenly matters, the model fails because it discarded that information.
The model learns to distinguish real signal from noise for your task, forgets the noise, and keeps accurate representations ten or twenty layers deep without degradation.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a dynamic graph where you control the signal-to-noise ratio: create a toy graph where some messages carry a clear pattern (e.g., 'this node always connects to high-value neighbors') and others are random. Stack many layers. Measure how accurately the model recovers the true pattern after 3, 10, and 20 layers. Compare naive stacking (which accumulates noise) to LAMP (which dissipates it). The demo should make it impossible to miss that LAMP keeps accuracy stable while naive stacking crashes.
demo.metric_eq: depth_stability = accuracy_at_layer_20 / accuracy_at_layer_3; a model with depth_stability close to 1.0 handles many layers well
demo.closing: The model should recover the true pattern even at layer 20, when naive stacking has become nearly random noise.
